newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesian army says foreigners provoke Timorese.
newsitem.headline: Indonesian army says foreigners provoke Timorese.

text.p: Indonesia's army chief in East Timor has said there were signs the presence of foreigners in the capital Dili had provoked demonstrations there by young East Timorese, the official Antara news agency reported on Thursday.

Violence broke out on Tuesday when an East Timorese soldier was beaten to death at Dili cathedral and 11 people were injured -- including Dili's police chief Lieutenant-Colonel Beno Kilapong -- in other incidents.

Antara quoted Colonel Mahidin Simbolon as saying a number of foreign journalists posing as tourists were present when Nobel peace laureate Bishop Carlos Belo returned to Dili from a European trip on Tuesday.
Belo received a rapturous welcome from tens of thousands of East Timorese lining the route from the airport to the town.

"At that time, the foreigners were allowed to photograph banners containing unfriendly writings, while local (Indonesian) journalists were not given the opportunity to take the same pictures," Simbolon was quoted as saying.
"This is one indication that the presence of foreigners is always used to do provocations," he said.

U.S. Congressman Patrick Kennedy, nephew of the late U.S. president John F. Kennedy, arrived in Dili on Tuesday on a two-day visit on the same flight as Belo, who had gone to Norway to accept his Nobel award.
Some foreign journalists had been accredited by Jakarta to visit East Timor over Christmas.

Antara said Simbolon identified the dead man as Corporal Alfredo Siga, who the colonel said was on Christmas leave. Residents said the soldier was beaten to death after being found with a pistol in the cathedral grounds.
Rumours had been circulating that an attempt would be made on Belo's life on his return from his European trip, during which he also met German Chancellor Helmut Kohl in Bonn and the Pope in Rome.
Special squads of Timorese Catholic youths wearing yellow T-shirts emblazoned with an image of Belo surrounded the bishop after he arrived.
"This morning I met the bishop and he expressed deep regret over the fatal incident," Simbolon told reporters on Wednesday night.
He said Second Lieutenant Abidin Tobba, from the army's information section in Dili, sustained serious head and stomach injuries when he was attacked with a blunt instrument.
Simbolon said Tobba was set upon by the crowd while he was photographing a banner reading "Viva Xanana", referring to jailed East Timorese resistance leader Xanana Gusmao.
Of the 11 injured, Simbolon confirmed only three were civilians.

East Timor's deputy police chief Colonel Atok Rismanto told Reuters on Thursday the Dili police chief, Kilapong, had been discharged from the town's military hospital. Three people were still being treated, he added.

Rismanto denied a Portuguese radio report that a soldier had been killed in a clash with people who had raised a flag of the Fretilin resistance movement near the municipal market in Dili on Christmas Day. "There was no such incident," he said.
Residents contacted were not able to confirm the incident.
Rismanto said there had been no arrests for Tuesday's violence.

Meanwhile, in a separate incident near Viqueque on Tuesday, Rismanto said most of the 46 people detained by police after what he said was an inter-clan clash had been released. "Only eight will be processed," he said.
East Timor remains unsettled more than 21 years after Indonesia invaded the former Portugese colony in December 1975 and declared it the country's 27th province the following year.
